goals: Retell the main events of the story in sequence, in your own words
Explain the themes of unshakeable faith and human kindness
Explain the irony of the ending and its effect on the reader
Describe Lencho and the postmaster with evidence from the story
Answer extract-based, short and long questions within the word limits

slides.narration: Welcome. Today we study A Letter to God by the Mexican writer G. L. Fuentes. Before anything else, please read the story itself in your textbook, First Flight. This lesson does not repeat the text. Instead we will understand it: the events, the themes, the characters, the irony at the end, and how to answer board questions on it.

slides.heading: How to use this lesson
bullets: Read the story once in *First Flight*, straight through, for enjoyment.
Then use these slides for the events, themes, characters and devices.
In answers, describe incidents **in your own words**; do not memorise lines.
Practise the extract questions, which use SOYL commentary on the story.
slides.narration: Here is the best way to study a literature lesson. First, read the story in your textbook, once, just to enjoy it. Then come back to these slides to understand its structure and meaning. When you write answers, describe incidents in your own words, because examiners reward understanding, not memorised lines. Finally, practise with our extract questions and short answers.

visual.alt: Table of facts about the story: author G. L. Fuentes, a Mexican writer; originally in Spanish; a short story with an ironic ending, set in a farming valley in rural Mexico; characters Lencho, his family, a postman and the postmaster.

slides.narration: The author, Gregorio López y Fuentes, was a Mexican writer who lived from eighteen ninety-seven to nineteen sixty-six. He wrote about the lives of farmers and villagers in rural Mexico. This story was first written in Spanish, and we read it in translation. It is set in a farming valley, and the money in the story is the peso, the Mexican currency.

slides.heading: The story in five stages
slides.body_md: Five stages, each a turn in Lencho's fortunes. (A SOYL summary, not the text.)

nodes.label: Hope: the crop needs one rain
Faith: a letter to God for 100 pesos
Irony: Lencho accuses the post office

visual.alt: Flow of the story in five stages: hope for rain, ruin by hail, a letter to God for a hundred pesos, the postmaster raising seventy pesos, and Lencho accusing the post office.
visual.caption: The story in five stages (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: The story moves in five clear stages. Hope, as a farmer waits for the one rain his crop needs. Ruin, when hail destroys that crop. Faith, when he writes to God for a hundred pesos. Kindness, when the postmaster raises seventy pesos to reply. And irony, when Lencho accuses the very people who helped him. Keep these five words in mind as a map.

slides.heading: Summary 1: hope, then ruin
slides.body_md: Lencho's family farm a valley where everything depends on the harvest. The maize is ripe and the crop looks excellent; it needs only one good rain. When rain finally arrives, Lencho is overjoyed and pictures the drops as money. But the wind rises and hail falls for about an hour, leaving the crop destroyed. By night the family fears a year of hunger.
slides.narration: In your own words, the first part is about hope turning into ruin. Lencho is a farmer whose whole year depends on one harvest. His crop is ripe and promising, and it needs just one good rain. When the rain begins, he is delighted and imagines the drops as money. Then hail falls for about an hour and destroys everything. The family now faces hunger.

slides.heading: Summary 2: a letter to God
slides.body_md: Grief does not turn into despair, because the family still trusts that God will help. Lencho, a farmer who can write, decides to ask God directly. On a Sunday he writes asking for a hundred pesos to replant and to feed his family until the next harvest, addresses the envelope to God, and posts it in town.
slides.narration: The second part is about faith. Even after the disaster, the family holds on to one hope: that God will help them. Lencho can write, so he decides to ask God directly. On a Sunday he writes a letter asking for a hundred pesos, enough to replant and to feed his family until the next harvest. He addresses it to God and posts it in town.

slides.heading: Summary 3: the post office responds
slides.body_md: A postman finds the address funny and shows it to the postmaster, who laughs too, but then grows serious, moved by a faith stronger than his own. Not wanting that faith to be crushed, he decides to reply. He collects money from his staff and friends and adds part of his own salary, but raises only seventy pesos. He sends it with a note signed simply *God*.
slides.narration: The third part is about kindness. At the post office the letter first causes laughter. But the postmaster soon becomes serious, because he is moved by such complete faith. He decides that it must not be crushed by silence. So he collects money from his staff and friends, adds part of his own salary, and manages seventy pesos. He signs the reply as God.

slides.heading: Summary 4: the ironic ending
slides.body_md: The next Sunday Lencho collects the envelope. He is not surprised to find money, but counting it makes him angry: sure that God cannot have sent less, he decides the missing thirty pesos were stolen. He writes again, asking God for the rest and warning God not to send it by post, because he suspects the post office staff.
slides.narration: The last part is the irony. When Lencho opens the envelope, he is calm, because he expected God to answer. But when he counts seventy pesos instead of a hundred, he is angry. Certain that God could not send less, he decides someone stole the rest. So he writes again, asking for the remaining money, and tells God not to use the post office, whose staff he now suspects.

slides.heading: Check: put the events in order
slides.narration: Your turn. Six events from the story are shuffled. Put them in the order they happen. Use the five stages, hope, ruin, faith, kindness and irony, as your guide.

slides.heading: Theme 1: faith
slides.body_md: Lencho's faith is total: he writes to God as if to a person who will reply, and he is calm when the reply comes. The story shows both sides of such faith.
columns:
**Faith as strength**

- keeps the family going after the storm
- moves the postmaster to act
- leads, in a roundabout way, to real help

**Faith as blindness**

- Lencho cannot imagine God sending less
- so he assumes people stole from him
- he never sees the kindness that saved him
slides.narration: The central theme is faith. Lencho believes so completely that he writes to God as he would to a person, and he is not surprised by the reply. This faith gives him strength after the storm, and it even inspires the postmaster. But it also blinds him. Because God cannot be wrong in his eyes, he assumes people must have cheated him.

slides.heading: Theme 2: irony, belief versus fact
slides.body_md: Situational irony: the outcome is the opposite of what we expect. Dramatic irony: the reader knows the truth that Lencho does not.
columns: **Expected:** a grateful farmer thanks God and, unknowingly, the kind people who helped.
**Actual:** the farmer accuses those very people of theft and asks God to bypass them.

rows: God read his letter and sent money.
The postmaster read it and organised the reply.
God sent the full hundred pesos.
Post office staff stole thirty pesos.
Post office staff gave their own money.
The staff are his only benefactors.

visual.alt: Two-column table contrasting what Lencho believes, that God sent a hundred pesos and the staff stole thirty, with what really happened, that the postmaster and staff collected seventy pesos from their own money.
visual.caption: The gap between belief and fact is the irony.

slides.narration: Irony is the heart of the ending. We expect Lencho to be grateful. Instead, he accuses the post office staff, the only people who actually helped him, of stealing. That is situational irony. There is also dramatic irony, because we, the readers, know where the money came from, while Lencho does not. The result is funny and sad at the same time.

slides.heading: A web of themes

rows: Lencho writes to God and expects a reply without doubt.
The helpers are accused of theft.
Strangers give their own money and seek no credit.
Rain brings joy; hail brings ruin.
One lost crop means a year of hunger.
Lencho cannot see the goodness of people around him.

visual.alt: Table of six themes of the story with where each appears: faith, irony, human kindness, nature as giver and destroyer, poverty and dependence, and gratitude versus suspicion.

slides.narration: Around faith and irony sit other themes. Human kindness, in strangers who give their own money and want no credit. Nature as both giver and destroyer. The poverty of a farmer for whom one lost crop means a year of hunger. And the contrast between gratitude and suspicion. In long answers, connect at least two themes to show depth.

slides.heading: Check: name the device
slides.narration: Check yourself. The reader knows the money came from the postmaster and his staff, but Lencho does not. What is this kind of irony called?

slides.heading: Character: Lencho
slides.body_md: Every trait in an answer needs an incident, described in your own words.

rows: He reads his land and the sky closely; his year's work is in the field.
He sees the first rain as money arriving.
He writes to God and is not surprised when money comes.
He asks only for what he needs to replant and survive.
He blames the post office for the missing thirty pesos.

visual.alt: Table of Lencho’s traits with evidence: hard-working, optimistic, deeply faithful, practical, and naive and suspicious.

slides.narration: Let us sketch Lencho. He is hard-working and experienced, watching his land and the sky closely. He is optimistic, seeing rain as money. His faith is deep and simple. He is practical, asking only for what he needs. But he is also naive and suspicious, blaming the post office for the shortfall. Notice that every trait is backed by an incident.

slides.heading: Character: the postmaster

rows: He laughs at first at a letter addressed to God.
He quickly grows serious and respects the faith behind it.
He gives part of his own salary.
He organises a collection from staff and friends.
He signs the reply as God and takes no credit.

visual.alt: Table of the postmaster’s traits with evidence: good-humoured, respectful of faith, generous, resourceful and humble.

slides.narration: Now the postmaster. He is good-humoured, laughing at first at the strange address. But he is also sensitive, quickly seeing the faith behind it and respecting it. He is generous, giving part of his salary, and resourceful, organising a collection. Above all he is humble, signing the reply as God. Many readers see him as the real hero of the story.

slides.heading: Was Lencho ungrateful?
columns:
**Yes, in effect**

- he insults the people who helped him
- he shows no doubt about his own judgement
- he demands the rest rather than giving thanks

**Not deliberately**

- he never learns who sent the money
- his anger comes from faith, not greed
- he asked only for what he needed
slides.narration: A favourite exam debate: was Lencho ungrateful? In effect, yes. He insults his helpers and demands the rest of the money. But he is not deliberately ungrateful, because he never learns the truth, and his anger comes from his faith, not greed. The best answers take a clear position and still acknowledge the other side.

slides.heading: Check: Lencho in the second letter
slides.narration: Try this. Which phrase best describes Lencho when he writes his second letter? Think about what he knows and what he does not know.

slides.heading: Narrative technique and language
bullets: **Third-person narrator:** we see Lencho's home and the post office, so we know more than Lencho.
**Comparison:** raindrops pictured as coins; hailstones as pearls (metaphor and simile).
**Contrast and reversal:** joy at rain → ruin by hail; kindness → accusation.
**Irony:** situational and dramatic, left without comment at the end.
**Plain, simple style** that suits a simple, sincere hero.
slides.narration: How does Fuentes tell the story? A third-person narrator shows us both Lencho’s home and the post office, so we know more than Lencho does. He uses comparisons, raindrops as coins and hailstones as pearls. He builds contrasts, joy then ruin, kindness then accusation. And he ends with irony, without any comment. The plain style suits a sincere, simple hero.

slides.heading: Spotting comparisons: SOYL's own examples
slides.body_md: A **simile** compares using *like* or *as*; a **metaphor** says one thing *is* another. These sentences are SOYL's own, to practise the device:
bullets: *The fireflies were tiny lanterns over the paddy.* — metaphor
*Her laugh rang out like a temple bell.* — simile
*The exam hall was an oven by noon.* — metaphor
slides.narration: Here are three sentences of our own to practise. The fireflies were tiny lanterns: a metaphor, because it says they are lanterns. Her laugh rang out like a temple bell: a simile, because it uses like. The exam hall was an oven: a metaphor again. In the story, Lencho turns raindrops into coins in the same way. Find that moment in your textbook.

slides.heading: Word meanings

rows: small balls of ice that fall like rain
insects that travel in swarms and destroy crops
the inner sense of right and wrong

visual.alt: Table of word meanings: crest, downpour, hailstones, locusts, conscience, amiable, correspondence, contentment and crooks.
visual.caption: Single words from the story with their meanings.

slides.narration: These words from the story often appear in questions. Crest means the top of a hill. A downpour is heavy rain. Locusts are insects that destroy crops in swarms. Conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong. Amiable means friendly. Correspondence is an exchange of letters. And crooks are cheats, the word Lencho uses for the post office staff.

slides.heading: Worked example: planning a 6-mark answer
slides.body_md: *Question:* *The postmaster is the real hero of the story.* Do you agree?
bullets: **Stand:** agree.
**Points + incidents:** respects faith instead of mocking it; collects money and gives his own salary; signs as God, seeking no credit.
**Link:** the irony of being called a thief makes his goodness stand out.
**Conclusion:** his humility and generosity make him the true hero.

visual.alt: Flow for planning a six-mark long answer: take a stand, give points with incidents in your own words, link to the theme, and conclude.

slides.narration: Here is how to plan a six mark answer. Take a clear stand: agree. Then give three points, each with an incident in your own words: he respects Lencho’s faith, he collects money and gives his own salary, and he signs as God. Link this to the irony of being called a thief. End with a one-line conclusion. That plan becomes about one hundred and twenty words.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Five stages: hope → ruin → faith → kindness → irony.
Lencho: hard-working, optimistic, deeply faithful, practical, naive and suspicious.
Postmaster: respectful, generous, resourceful, humble: the quiet hero.
Themes: faith (strength and blindness), irony, human kindness, nature, poverty.
Read the story in *First Flight*; write about it in your own words.

slides.narration: Let us sum up. The story moves from hope to ruin, to faith, to kindness, and finally to irony. Lencho is hard-working and faithful but naive. The postmaster is the quiet hero, generous and humble. The themes are faith as both strength and blindness, irony, kindness, nature, and poverty. And remember: read the story in your textbook, and write about it in your own words.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Extract questions: answer from the passage first; quote at most a word or two.
3-mark answers (40–50 words): point + incident + explanation.
6-mark answers (100–120 words): stand → 3 points with incidents → link to theme → conclusion.
Facts that are often confused: 100 pesos asked, 70 received; the postman hands over the envelope; the reply is signed *God*.
Do not call the postmaster dishonest or Lencho greedy; explain the irony instead.
slides.narration: Exam tips. In extract questions, answer from the passage first. In three mark answers, give a point, an incident and a short explanation. In six mark answers, take a stand and support it with three incidents. Get the facts right: a hundred pesos asked, seventy received, signed God. And never call the postmaster dishonest or Lencho greedy. Explain the irony instead.

sections.heading: 1. About the story and the author
sections.body_md:
**Read the story itself in your textbook, *First Flight* (NCERT).** This lesson is SOYL's explanation and analysis; it does not reproduce the text.

*A Letter to God* is a short story by **G. L. Fuentes** (Gregorio López y Fuentes, 1897–1966), a Mexican novelist, poet and journalist who wrote about rural Mexico and its farming and indigenous communities; his best-known novel is *El Indio* (1935). The story was written in Spanish and is read in English translation. It is set in a farming valley; the currency, pesos, places it in rural Mexico.

sections.heading: 2. Summary (in SOYL's words)
sections.body_md:
**Hope and ruin.** Lencho's family farm a valley and depend entirely on their harvest. The maize is ripe and needs only one good rain. When it rains, Lencho is overjoyed and pictures the drops as money, but a storm of hail lasting about an hour destroys the crop, and the family fears a year of hunger.

**Faith.** The family still trusts that God will help. Lencho, who can write, asks God for a hundred pesos to replant and feed his family until the next harvest, addresses the envelope to God and posts it.

**Kindness.** At the post office, the postman and the postmaster first laugh; the postmaster then grows serious, moved by the farmer's faith. To protect that faith he replies, collecting money from his staff and friends and from his own salary. He raises seventy pesos and signs the note *God*.

**Irony.** Lencho is not surprised to receive money, but is angry that thirty pesos are missing. He writes again asking God for the rest and not to send it by post, because he suspects the post office staff.

sections.heading: 3. Themes
sections.body_md:
- **Faith:** total, simple faith gives Lencho strength and inspires the postmaster, but also blinds him to human goodness.
- **Irony:** the helpers are accused of theft (situational); the reader knows what Lencho does not (dramatic).
- **Human kindness:** strangers give quietly, seeking no credit.
- **Nature as giver and destroyer:** rain brings joy, hail brings ruin.
- **Poverty and dependence:** one lost crop means a year of hunger.
- **Gratitude and suspicion:** Lencho cannot see the kindness around him.

**Message:** faith in God and trust in people should go together; kindness is often unrecognised, yet worth doing.

sections.heading: 4. Characters
sections.body_md:
**Lencho:** a hard-working, experienced farmer; optimistic; deeply and simply faithful; practical in his request; but naive and suspicious, so that he unknowingly wrongs his helpers.

**The postmaster:** good-humoured, then sensitive and respectful of faith; generous (gives his own salary); resourceful (organises the collection); humble (signs as God). He is often seen as the real hero.

**Others:** Lencho's wife and children share the family's hope for rain and its grief after the storm; the postman finds the letter amusing and hands over the reply.

sections.heading: 7. Answering exam questions
sections.body_md:
**Extract-based (5 marks):** the board prints a passage from the story; SOYL practice uses commentary passages instead. Answer from the passage, then from your knowledge of the story.

**Short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words):** point + incident + explanation.

**Long answers (6 marks, 100–120 words):** a clear stand; three points with incidents in your own words; a link to a theme or the irony; a one-line conclusion. Extrapolation tasks (diary of the postmaster, Lencho's letter after learning the truth) must stay consistent with the characters.

Practise with the real textbook passages from *First Flight*.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** reference-to-context extract (5), short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words) and long answers (6 marks, 100–120 words) from *First Flight* (CBSE 2026-27, Section C).

**How marks are awarded:** content (relevant incidents, accurately used), interpretation (a clear, supported view), and expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Wrong amounts: Lencho asks for 100 pesos and receives 70.
2. Saying the postmaster handed over the letter: the postman did; the postmaster watched.
3. Calling the postmaster dishonest, or Lencho greedy.
4. Retelling the story instead of answering the question asked.
5. Quoting long lines from memory instead of explaining in your own words.

**Remember:** read the story in your textbook, *First Flight*.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) A good rain means a good harvest and income for him.

**(b)** (d) to make the coming disaster feel more painful

**(c)** hailstorm

**(d)** He is an experienced farmer who understands his fields and the weather well.

questions.passage_md: Before the storm, Fuentes takes time to build up Lencho's hope. Here is a farmer who reads his land and his sky with the eye of long experience, waiting for the single good rain that will secure his harvest. When the rain begins, his delight is so great that he pictures the falling drops as money, a picture that shows how closely a poor farmer's income is tied to the weather. The reader shares his excitement, and that is exactly the point: the higher the hope, the harder the fall that follows. The same sky that seemed to bless the family is about to betray it.

children.stem_md: Why does Lencho picture the raindrops as money?

options.text_md: He has found coins in his field.
A good rain means a good harvest and income for him.
He wants to sell rainwater in town.
He is dreaming about winning a prize.

children.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A good rain means a good harvest and income for him. For a farmer, rain turns into crops and crops into money; the picture links the weather directly to his earnings.

children.stem_md: According to the commentary, why does the writer build up Lencho's hope before the storm?

questions.passage_md: The final twist of the story turns gratitude upside down. Lencho writes again, asking God for the rest of the money and warning God not to use the post, because he believes the post office staff are thieves. questions.passage_md: Nature plays two roles in this story. At first it is the giver: the family's whole year depends on rain, and the first drops feel like a reward. Within moments it becomes the destroyer. Strong wind and hail sweep across the valley for about an hour and leave the crop in ruins, with nothing left to harvest. That helplessness explains why his hope turns so completely towards God.

He then signs the reply as God, seeking no credit, and is quietly pleased when his plan works. Lencho is the central character, but he only receives; the postmaster gives without being asked. questions.stem_md: Explain the irony in *A Letter to God* and how it shapes the story's message. Answer in 100–120 words.

answer.model_answer_md: The story ends in situational irony. Lencho asks God for money, and the postmaster, moved by his faith, collects seventy pesos from his staff, his friends and his own salary. Instead of being grateful, Lencho is angry that thirty pesos are missing and warns God not to use the post because the employees are thieves. The only people who helped him are accused of stealing from him. There is also dramatic irony, since the reader knows the truth while Lencho does not. This irony carries the message: blind faith can make us overlook the goodness of ordinary people, and kindness often goes unrecognised. The ending is both funny and sad.

answer.model_answer_md:
Sunday, 9 p.m.

Today I learnt how strange kindness can be. The farmer who wrote to God came again and wrote a second letter at our counter. I opened it as soon as he left, expecting thanks. Instead, he complained that thirty pesos were missing and asked God to send the rest, but not by post, because, he says, my staff are thieves! I laughed at first, and then felt a little hurt. My colleagues gave from their small salaries, and so did I. Still, his faith is untouched, and that was what we wanted to protect. Perhaps goodness should not need thanks. Tomorrow I must decide whether to tell the others.

questions.stem_md: Suppose Lencho later discovers that the money came from the postmaster and his staff. Write the letter he might send to the postmaster, in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Letter format (salutation, body, close). Content: recognition of the truth, apology for the accusation, thanks, a changed understanding of how help came, a promise. The tone must suit a humble, honest farmer.

answer.model_answer_md:
Respected Sir,

I am the farmer from the valley who wrote to God after the hail ruined my corn. I have just learnt that the seventy pesos I received came from you, your staff and your friends, not from heaven directly. I am deeply ashamed of my second letter. In my anger I called your employees thieves, when in truth they had given me their own money. Please forgive me and tell them that I am sorry. I now understand that God answered my prayer through your kind hearts. When my new crop is harvested, I will repay every peso and bring you the first of my corn.

Yours gratefully,
Lencho

questions.stem_md: Faith can give strength, but blind faith can make us unfair to others. Discuss with reference to *A Letter to God*, in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Two-sided discussion: faith as strength (hope after the storm; inspiring the postmaster) and as blindness (false accusation). Conclude with a balanced message, using events in your own words.

answer.model_answer_md: Lencho's faith gives him strength at his lowest point. When the hail destroys his crop and his family fears hunger, it is faith that stops him from giving up and leads him to ask God for help. That same faith moves the postmaster, who wishes he believed as strongly. Yet Lencho's faith is blind as well as strong. Because he cannot imagine God sending less than he asked for, he concludes that people stole from him, and he insults the very men who helped him. The story suggests that faith in God and trust in people should go together. Faith that sees no goodness in humans can turn hope into injustice.

questions.stem_md: How does *A Letter to God* show a farmer's complete dependence on nature? Answer in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Trace the dependence: the year's work → the need for rain → joy at rain → destruction by hail → fear of hunger → turning to God. Conclude on fragility and faith.

answer.model_answer_md: The story shows that a small farmer's whole life depends on the weather. Lencho's family has worked all year, and only one good rain is needed for a rich harvest. When rain comes, Lencho is overjoyed and sees each drop as money. But nature changes in a moment: a storm of hail falls for about an hour and ruins the entire crop. With no savings or other income, the family now fears hunger for a whole year. Their only hope is God. Through this sudden reversal, Fuentes shows how fragile the farmer's existence is, and why his faith matters so much to him.

questions.stem_md: Who wrote *A Letter to God*?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** G. L. Fuentes. The story is by the Mexican writer G. L. (Gregorio López y) Fuentes. Frost, Chekhov and Maxwell wrote other texts in the Class 10 books.

questions.stem_md: In which currency does Lencho ask for money?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** pesos. He asks for pesos, the currency of Mexico.

questions.stem_md: Which crop of Lencho's is ruined by the hail?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** corn. His field of ripe corn (maize) is destroyed.

questions.stem_md: Who hands the envelope with the money to Lencho?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the postman. The postman hands it over while the postmaster watches from his office.

questions.stem_md: The ending, in which Lencho accuses his helpers of theft, is an example of…
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** irony. An outcome opposite to what is expected is irony.

questions.stem_md: Which is the central theme of the story?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** faith. Lencho's unquestioning faith in God drives every major event.

questions.stem_md: Which quality of the postmaster is shown when he gives part of his own salary?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** generosity. Giving his own money for a stranger is generous.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is the best description of Lencho's behaviour in his second letter?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** unknowingly ungrateful. He does not know who helped him, so his ingratitude is unknowing, not deliberate; he certainly is not thankful or indifferent.

questions.stem_md: The reader knows where the money came from, but Lencho does not. This is called…
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** dramatic irony. When the audience knows something a character does not, it is dramatic irony.

questions.stem_md: From which point of view is the story told?

options.text_md: the postmaster, in the first person

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a third-person narrator. An outside narrator tells the story, describing Lencho, his family and the post office.

questions.stem_md: The postmaster is described as *amiable*. This means he is…
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** friendly and pleasant. *Amiable* = good-natured, friendly.

questions.stem_md: Why does the postmaster decide to reply to Lencho's letter?

options.text_md: so that Lencho's faith in God is not shaken

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** so that Lencho's faith in God is not shaken. He admires the faith and wants to protect it.

questions.stem_md: Which message does the story most strongly suggest?

options.text_md: Farmers should never trust the weather.
Letters should always be sent by registered post.
Kindness often goes unrecognised, even by those it helps.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Kindness often goes unrecognised, even by those it helps. The ending shows the helpers being accused instead of thanked: kindness unrecognised.

questions.stem_md: Lencho's view of raindrops as coins is a comparison. Which of these SOYL-written sentences uses the same kind of device?

options.text_md: The fireflies were tiny lanterns floating over the paddy.
Ravi shouted loudly at the umpire.
We ate rice and dal for lunch.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The fireflies were tiny lanterns floating over the paddy. Only the first sentence compares one thing to another (fireflies → lanterns), as Lencho compares raindrops to coins; the others are literal statements.

questions.stem_md: Lencho asked God for ___ pesos but received only ___ pesos.
questions.solution_md: He asked for **a hundred** (100) and received **seventy** (70).

questions.stem_md: Lencho wrote his first letter and later collected the reply on a ___.
questions.solution_md: Both happen on a **Sunday**, his day off from the fields.

questions.stem_md: The reply that reached Lencho was signed with a single word: ___.
questions.solution_md: It was signed **God**.

questions.stem_md: When the result of an action is the opposite of what we expect, as at the end of this story, the device is called situational ___.
questions.solution_md: Situational **irony**: Lencho's helpers are accused of theft.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lencho is not surprised when he finds money in the envelope.

**Reason (R):** He has complete faith that God will answer his letter.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and his certain faith is exactly why he shows no surprise.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The postmaster signs the reply as God.

**Reason (R):** The postmaster laughs when he first sees the letter.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but his first laughter does not explain the signature; he signs as God to keep Lencho's faith intact.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The postmaster sends Lencho the full hundred pesos.

**Reason (R):** The postmaster collects money from his employees, his friends and his own salary.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: he could collect only just over half (seventy pesos). R is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lencho believes the post office employees took part of the money.

**Reason (R):** The post office employees are shown to be dishonest in the story.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: the employees contributed their own money; they are generous, not dishonest. That gap is the irony.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the rain at the beginning of the story makes Lencho happy.
questions.solution_md: **True.** He is overjoyed, because a good rain means a good harvest.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the postman refuses to show the letter to his boss.
questions.solution_md: **False.** The postman takes the letter to the postmaster, laughing.

questions.stem_md: True or false: Lencho writes his second letter at the post office.
questions.solution_md: **True.** He asks for paper and ink at the counter and writes it there before posting it.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the postmaster collects the money mainly to become famous in the town.
questions.solution_md: **False.** He hides his part completely by signing as God; his motive is to protect Lencho's faith.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the events of the story in the correct order.

options.text_md: Lencho writes again, accusing the post office staff.
Lencho writes to God asking for a hundred pesos.
Lencho receives seventy pesos and becomes angry.
A long-awaited rain begins to fall on Lencho's field.
The postmaster collects money from his staff, friends and salary.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (c) → (b) → (f) → (d) → (a). Rain → hail → first letter → collection → seventy pesos and anger → second letter.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the postmaster's actions in the order in which they happen.

options.text_md: He laughs at the letter addressed to God.
He watches with satisfaction as Lencho receives it.
He collects money for the reply.
He grows serious and admires the writer's faith.
He signs the reply as God.
He decides to answer the letter.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (a) → (d) → (f) → (c) → (e) → (b). Laughter → respect → decision → collection → signature → satisfaction.
